# Introduction

Alpine ecosystems are among the most vulnerable to climate change [@IPCCSR2019HM]. Resurveys across mountain regions have documented upslope range shifts, increasing summit species richness, and changes in the composition of high-elevation vegetation [@Gottfried2012NatClimChange; @Rumpf2018PNAS; @Lamprecht2018NewPhytol], while satellite observations show widespread greening of alpine landscapes [@Carlson2017ERL]. Much of this change reflects the expansion of species that gain a competitive advantage as environmental constraints relax. Examples include woody shrub expansion in Arctic and alpine tundra [@MyersSmith2011ERL; @Bjorkman2018Nature] and the encroachment of grasses and tall forbs into snowbed communities as the snow-free season lengthens [@Grabherr2003book; @Dullinger2003AAA]. In Japanese alpine ecosystems, dwarf bamboo (*Sasa* spp., hereafter *Sasa*) represents a prominent example. *Sasa* forms dense evergreen stands that exclude subordinate species, and its expansion into snowbed meadows has been associated with earlier snowmelt and reductions in plant species richness [@Kudo2011EcoEvo]. Snowbed vegetation has recovered following experimental removal of *Sasa* [@Kudo2017AlpBot]. Understanding where and how rapidly *Sasa* expands is therefore directly relevant to alpine plant conservation.

Snowmelt timing is a central environmental factor for alpine vegetation because it determines the onset and duration of the growing season and is closely linked to growing conditions such as soil temperature and moisture [@Wipf2010PolarRes; @Wahren2005GCB]. Spatial scale matters here. Snowmelt varies with microtopography over distances of a few to tens of metres, and alpine vegetation forms a fine mosaic of communities along these snowmelt gradients. Linking changes in alpine plant distributions to environmental conditions therefore requires simultaneous observations of vegetation and snowmelt at approximately 1 m resolution. Field plots capture this scale but lack continuous spatial coverage. Satellites provide decades of snow and vegetation observations at 10–30 m resolution, but cannot resolve community mosaics or movements of patch boundaries. Ground-based time-lapse cameras fill this gap. Repeated daily photographs from a fixed viewpoint allow automated extraction of both per-pixel snowmelt dates and vegetation maps at sub-metre ground resolution [@IdeOguma2013EcolInfom; @Okamoto2024RSEC]. The two approaches are therefore complementary: the expansion patterns that satellites record over decades and at scales of tens of metres can be examined alongside the metre-scale processes that underlie them.

*Sasa* expands through two contrasting dispersal processes [@Suyama2000MolEcol; @Kudo2011EcoEvo]. The first is the gradual advance of patch fronts through rhizome elongation; where this process dominates, expansion may be limited by the rate of dispersal rather than by the extent of environmentally suitable habitat. The second is establishment from seed following mass or partial flowering [@Miyazaki2009JPlantRes; @Mizuki2014PLOS], which can bypass local distance constraints and form new patches. Conservation planning requires information on both: where environmental conditions permit *Sasa* to establish if seeds arrive, and how far existing fronts can actually reach. For the former question, habitat suitability models, statistical frameworks relating species presence to environmental conditions, have been widely used in conservation planning and projections of distributional change [@Guisan1998JVS; @Larson2004EcolModel; @Thomas2004Nature; @Gallien2010DD; @Amagai2022AVS]. Projecting suitability maps without accounting for dispersal constraints, however, can greatly overestimate establishment area [@Engler2009DD; @Engler2012Ecography]. Answering the latter question requires distribution maps of the same area at two or more times. Comparing two maps reveals the cells in which establishment actually occurred. These observed transitions can then be modelled directly as a function of environment and distance from the existing front, projecting expansion as a process rather than as a reassessment of a static suitability map.

Here, we apply this approach to *Sasa* on the western slope of Mt. Tateyama in the northern Japanese Alps. Plot resurveys on the nearby Murodo-daira plateau have documented 44–260% expansion of *Sasa* patches over 38 years [@Yoshida2016SasaTateyama]. Using 10 years of time-lapse imagery, we (i) map *Sasa* distributions in 2012 and 2021 at 1 m resolution and quantify gross expansion, gross loss, and net change; (ii) characterise the snowmelt regime and its decadal trend for every pixel; (iii) fit a habitat suitability model of environmental potential (Model A) and an establishment model of observed transitions (Model B) to estimate how strongly snowmelt regime and topography are associated with *Sasa* distribution and establishment, while accounting for proximity to existing patches; (iv) project establishment to 2030 under explicit snowmelt scenarios using stochastic simulations based on the establishment model; and (v) identify the alpine communities most exposed to near-term expansion.
